```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(scans)
```

The built-in scans know about tool calls, errors, and run endings. They know
nothing about your application. Whether a support assistant really issued the
refund it announced, or whether a policy assistant answered without a source,
depends on which tools and phrases your application uses. A custom scanner is
how you teach scans one such rule.

This article works through two scanners that ship as examples:

- **Unsupported action claim** (support assistant): the assistant says an
  action was done, and the trajectory records no successful call to the tool
  that performs it.
- **Answer without retrieved support** (retrieval application): the assistant
  gives a substantive answer after retrieval failed or returned nothing, or in
  an exchange whose recorded commons provenance has no trusted or cited
  source.

Everything here is deterministic and runs offline. No model is called when you
scan, validate, or browse the results.

> The conversations and review decisions used below were written for this
> recipe. They are not production conversations and nobody reviewed them
> independently. The rates they produce show how validation works. They say
> nothing about how these scanners would do on your application.

## Define a scanner

A scanner is a function and a few declared facts. `scanner()` takes a name, the
function, a description, the evidence the function needs, a version, and
settings. The function is called once per trajectory with that trajectory's
rows and the settings:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
scanner(
  "unsupported_action_claim",
  function(trajectory, settings) {
    # trajectory$info, $turns, $events, $evaluations, $losses
    # settings$actions
  },
  description = "The assistant said an action was done with no successful call to the tool that performs it.",
  required_evidence = "Assistant text, and tool calls and results with call identities, without capture losses.",
  severity = "error",
  settings = list(actions = actions)
)
```

It must return one of two things:

- `scanner_findings()` when it could assess the trajectory. Zero findings
  means "assessed, nothing found".
- `scanner_unassessed("insufficient_evidence", reason)` or
  `scanner_unassessed("not_applicable", reason)` when it could not.

That distinction is the scanner author's main responsibility. If tool calls
were not captured, "no refund call is recorded" proves nothing, and the honest
answer is insufficient evidence. A scanner that returns nothing at all is
recorded as a failure, never as a clean result.

The two example scanners are ordinary R files installed with the package. Read
them before going further; both are short.

```{r}
source(system.file("examples", "domain-scanners.R", package = "scans"))
source(system.file("examples", "domain-scanner-cases.R", package = "scans"))

claims <- unsupported_action_claim_scanner()
claims$name
claims$required_evidence
names(claims$settings$actions)
claims$settings$actions$refund
```

`unsupported_action_claim_scanner()` is a small function that returns a
scanner, so the application owner can pass their own tool names and claim
phrases. The defaults suit the fictional support assistant used here.

A phrase counts as a claim only in a sentence that is not a question and has
no "not", "never", "cannot", or "n't" before it, so "I have not issued a
refund yet" and "Have you already cancelled the order?" are not claims. That
removes the obvious negated and interrogative forms. It is still phrase
matching: a quoted claim, a conditional such as "once your refund is
processed", and a paraphrase the pattern does not list are all read wrongly.

## Run it and read the assessments

Pass scanners to `assess_trajectory_scans()` through `scanners`. Nothing is
registered globally: a scanner runs in the calls you give it to.

```{r}
support <- support_bundle()
result <- assess_trajectory_scans(
  support,
  scans = "unsupported_action_claim",
  scanners = claims
)
result$assessments[c("trajectory_id", "status")]
```

Each trajectory gets one assessment. Read the statuses before the findings:

```{r}
unassessed <- result$assessments[
  result$assessments$status == "insufficient_evidence",
]
unassessed$reason
unassessed$limitations[[1]]
```

That conversation contains a refund claim, but its tool calls were not
exported. The scanner declines to judge it. It is not counted as clean.

Findings have the same columns as built-in findings and cite events in the
trajectory. scans checks every reference: a finding that cites an event
outside its trajectory turns the whole result for that scanner and trajectory
into an `execution_failure`.

```{r}
result$findings[c("trajectory_id", "event_id", "label")]
result$findings$explanation[[1]]
result$findings$event_ids[[1]]
```

Omit `scans` to run the built-in scans too. Their results are identical with
or without custom scanners.

## Collect reviewed cases

A finding is a claim by the scanner. Before relying on it you need cases a
person has judged, including trajectories the scanner did *not* flag, since
only those can reveal what it misses.

The review functions are the ones described in
`vignette("reviewed-examples")`. Save an investigation with the scanner, open a
case on a finding or on a whole trajectory, and record a decision:

```{r}
saved <- investigation_snapshot(
  support,
  application = "Support assistant",
  scans = "unsupported_action_claim",
  scanners = claims
)
finding <- saved$analysis$findings$finding_id[[1]]
case <- review_case(saved, "support/refund-failed", finding_id = finding)
case <- review_decision(
  case, "confirmed", reviewer = "Recipe author",
  rationale = "The only refund call failed, and the assistant still said it was issued."
)
review_status(case)$status
```

Use `"confirmed"` for a valid finding, `"rejected"` for an invalid finding or
for an unflagged trajectory that is correctly clean, and `"missed"` for
something the scanner should have found, citing the event. `"uncertain"` and
`"insufficient_capture"` record that the reviewer could not judge.

`support_reviewed_cases()` builds twelve such cases this way and puts them in a
scanner example set with a development and a test split. Each conversation
belongs to one split.

```{r}
examples <- support_reviewed_cases(claims)
table(examples$splits)
```

The two splits have different jobs:

- **Development** cases are for building the scanner. Read the errors, change
  the scanner, run again, as often as you like.
- **Test** cases are held out. Look at them once the scanner is settled. If a
  test result leads you to change the scanner, those cases have become
  development cases and you need new held-out ones.

## Validate on development cases

`validate_scanner()` runs the scanner on each case's retained evidence and
compares the result with the adjudicated judgment.

```{r}
validation <- validate_scanner(claims, examples)
development <- validation$summary[validation$summary$split == "development", ]
t(development[c(
  "n_cases", "scored", "true_positive", "false_positive", "false_negative",
  "true_negative", "precision", "precision_denominator", "recall",
  "recall_denominator", "scanner_unassessed", "reviewer_uncertain",
  "not_adjudicated"
)])
```

Seven development cases, six scored. The seventh is a case the reviewer marked
uncertain: the cancellation tool answered `pending_review`, and whether that
counts as cancelled is a policy question. It is reported separately and is not
a negative. Precision is one of two flagged cases; recall is one of two
reviewed positives.

The per-case table says which cases those are and where to look:

```{r}
cases <- validation$cases
wrong <- cases[
  cases$split == "development" &
    cases$outcome %in% c("false_positive", "false_negative"),
]
wrong[c("trajectory_id", "judgment", "outcome")]
wrong$review_event_ids
```

Open the evidence for each. `case` is the position in the example set, so the
reviewer's rationale and the cited text are one step away:

```{r}
events <- trajectory_events(support)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(wrong))) {
  reviewed <- examples$cases[[wrong$case[[i]]]]
  cat(
    wrong$outcome[[i]], "\n",
    "  text:   ", events$text[events$event_id %in% wrong$review_event_ids[[i]]], "\n",
    "  review: ", reviewed$decisions[[1]]$rationale, "\n",
    sep = ""
  )
}
```

The false positive repeats what the customer was told. The false negative is a
paraphrase the ticket pattern does not cover.

## Change the scanner and run again

The paraphrase is fixable with a phrase. Add it, and give the scanner a new
version so saved findings and validation results say which detector produced
them.

```{r}
actions <- claims$settings$actions
actions$ticket$claim <- paste0(
  actions$ticket$claim,
  "|logged (this|it|that) with"
)
claims_v2 <- unsupported_action_claim_scanner(actions, version = "2")

validation_v2 <- validate_scanner(claims_v2, examples)
as.data.frame(validation_v2$summary[
  validation_v2$summary$split == "development",
  c("scan_version", "true_positive", "false_positive", "false_negative",
    "precision", "precision_denominator", "recall", "recall_denominator")
])
```

Recall on development cases is now two of two. The false positive remains: a
phrase list cannot tell a claim from a quotation. That is a known limit of
this scanner, and it is worth writing down rather than tuning around.

The cases were reviewed against version 1. Validation reruns the scanner you
pass on the evidence each case retained, and records both versions:

```{r}
unique(validation_v2$cases[c("scan_version", "reviewed_scan_version")])
```

## Check on held-out cases

Now look at the test split, once.

```{r}
test <- validation_v2$summary[validation_v2$summary$split == "test", ]
t(test[c(
  "n_cases", "scored", "true_positive", "false_positive", "false_negative",
  "true_negative", "precision", "precision_denominator", "recall",
  "recall_denominator", "scanner_unassessed", "insufficient_evidence"
)])
as.data.frame(validation_v2$cases[
  validation_v2$cases$split == "test",
  c("trajectory_id", "judgment", "assessment", "outcome")
])
```

The test split shows two errors of kinds the development cases did not
contain. One test conversation says "I have sent the money back", a
paraphrase of the refund action; the development paraphrase was of the ticket
action, and version 2 covers only that one. Another states refund policy in
words that match the claim pattern; the development false positive was a
quotation. The fixture cases were written to include both, so this shows what
a held-out check can catch, not how often it happens. The conversation with no
exported tool calls is counted as unassessed, with the scanner's own reason:

```{r}
validation_v2$cases$assessment_reason[
  validation_v2$cases$outcome == "scanner_unassessed"
]
```

Do not add "sent the money back" to the pattern now and report the test rates
again. Record the result, move those cases to development if you want to use
them, and review new held-out cases.

## A second scanner on the same interface

The retrieval scanner uses the same two return values. It needs retrieval
results or provenance records, so it has two ways of not assessing a
conversation.

```{r}
unsupported <- answer_without_support_scanner(retrieval_tools = "search_docs")
retrieval <- assess_trajectory_scans(
  retrieval_bundle(),
  scans = "answer_without_support",
  scanners = unsupported
)
unassessed <- retrieval$assessments[
  !startsWith(retrieval$assessments$status, "assessed"),
]
unassessed[c("trajectory_id", "status")]
unassessed$reason
```

A greeting with no retrieval call is `not_applicable`. A conversation whose
tool results were not exported is `insufficient_evidence`, and so is one with
a retrieval call whose result is not recorded or whose commons provenance was
lost. Neither status is a clean negative. Note the blind spot this leaves: an
assistant that never calls retrieval and answers from nothing is "not
applicable" to this scanner, not flagged by it.

Provenance records are read against their exchange. The scanner uses each
turn's `round_index` when the trajectory records rounds, as commons data does,
and otherwise treats each user turn that is not a tool result and not marked
`commons_internal` as a new exchange; this is the rule scans' route analysis
uses. The answer a record describes is the last substantive assistant text in
its exchange. Without `round_index`, a user turn the application injects
without marking it is taken for a new question, and an exchange with two long
answers gives one finding. A record whose exchange index is missing or
malformed is not used.

```{r}
retrieval_examples <- retrieval_reviewed_cases(unsupported)
retrieval_validation <- validate_scanner(unsupported, retrieval_examples)
t(retrieval_validation$summary[c(
  "split", "n_cases", "scored", "true_positive", "false_positive",
  "false_negative", "true_negative", "precision", "precision_denominator",
  "recall", "recall_denominator", "scanner_unassessed",
  "insufficient_evidence", "not_applicable", "reviewer_uncertain"
)])
```

A rate whose denominator is zero is `NA`, and `precision_note` or
`recall_note` says why. A scanner that throws on a case is counted under
`execution_failure`, inside `scanner_unassessed`.

## What the numbers do and do not justify

They justify a narrow statement: on these reviewed cases, this version of the
scanner agreed with the reviewers this often, and here are the cases where it
did not.

They do not justify more than that.

- **They are not production rates.** Reviewed cases are chosen, not sampled.
  A scanner with perfect precision on twelve chosen cases can be wrong often
  on real traffic.
- **Small denominators move a lot.** One case changes a rate of one in two to
  two in two. Report the counts next to the rates, as the summary does.
- **Unscored cases are not successes.** A scanner that could not assess a
  third of the cases has not been validated on that third.
- **A finding is not an application-quality target.** These scanners say that
  a recorded conversation matches a rule. They do not say the answer was
  wrong, and the absence of findings does not say the application is good.
  Keep detector validation separate from any measure of answer quality, and
  do not optimise the application to make findings disappear.
- **The fixture cases here are illustrations.** Replace them with cases from
  your own application, reviewed by someone who did not write the scanner.

## Save, reopen, and browse

Custom findings and assessments are saved with an investigation as data. The
scanner function is not saved.

```{r}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
write_investigation(saved, path)
reopened <- read_investigation(path)
table(reopened$analysis$assessments$status)
reopened$manifest$scanner_versions
```

A reopened investigation shows the saved custom results without the function.
Running the scanner again needs it, and scans says so:

```{r, error=TRUE}
investigation_snapshot(reopened$bundle, scans = reopened$settings$scans)
```

The app takes the same `scanners` argument. Custom scanners appear with the
built-in scans under Options, their findings appear in the overview and the
transcript, and each trajectory's Assessments panel shows their status and
reason. Custom scanners are deterministic functions, so browsing never calls a
model.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
scans_app(support, scanners = list(claims_v2))
```
